Children’s Literature
Children’s literature has existed for a relatively 
short time, and has played a signiﬁcant role in 
education only since the 19th century (though 
examples of children’s literature in Europe have 
been documented as early as the 17th century, 
because that is when such literature began to 
be written, speciﬁcally in Germany). But these 
were only preliminary attempts to bring this 
type of literature to the attention of the broader 
public. It was only during that period that chil-
dren began to be perceived as individual human 
beings with cultural needs of their own (Shavit 
1996). Before that time students’ reading mate-
rials were based mainly on a selection of Clas-
sical sources. The new stress on the importance 
of a special literature for children was founded 
on ethical principles and ideals.
Children’s literature is, of course, written 
for an audience consisting of children; it is 
therefore subject to certain didactic instructions 
and restrictions. However, because the works 
are usually chosen according to the tastes of 
parents and educators, it may also contain ele-
ments that address an adult audience, especially 
allusions to other texts. 
It is difﬁcult to delimit children’s literature 
by age; researchers tend to take it to include 
works intended more-or-less for the entire class 
of people included in the term ‘children’. Gold-
berg (1956) deﬁned children’s literature as a 
branch of prose and poetry whose contents 
and style are adapted to the understanding of 
children between the ages of ﬁve and about 
thirteen. This deﬁnition extends the concept in 
the direction of youth literature. Others deﬁne 
youth literature as works intended for ages 
twelve to seventeen. Some divide literature for 
non-adults into literature for small children 
(for infants and children in kindergarten and 
lower primary school grades), grade-school-age 
literature (ages eight to twelve) and adolescent 
literature (ages thirteen to seventeen or even 
eighteen).
One issue that has been the subject of schol-
arly attention is the nature of the difference 
between children’s and adult literature. Baruch 
(1985) focuses on two differences. One is age: 
certainly a two-year-old child’s vocabulary and 
experience differ from those of an eight-year-
old, and a ten-year-old’s differ from both, but 
they all differ in vocabulary and experience 
from adults. The second difference is that chil-
dren’s literature contains implicit or direct edu-
cational elements in keeping with the norms of 
the period in which the works were composed. 
Most scholars claim that anyone who writes 
for children must take their unique experiential 
world into consideration and that therefore this 
literature must adapt itself in style and con-
tent to children’s conceptual world. Texts for 
infants usually contain short, rhythmic poems, 
whose language is simple and minimalistic (for 
example, the poems of Fanya Bergstein), occa-
sionally with onomatopoeic elements and short 
and simple messages to which a young child 
can relate. It is an age when children are pre-
sented adapted legends and folk tales. The 
literature for children between the ages of nine 
and twelve or thirteen consists mostly of stories 
of youth groups, young detectives, and ‘Dear 
Diary’. For adolescents writers of children’s 
literature compose stories that relate to the 
problems of that age, whose precise age limits, 
however, are not easy to delineate. Baruch 
and Fruchtman (1982, as well as Cohen 1988; 
Regev 1985) note that the values promoted in 
children’s literature, and, in consequence, also 
the language, have changed over the years, in 
step with the changes that have taken place 
in opinions and style, and in the perception of 
children and their needs in different periods. 
According to Goldberg (1956) the unique his-
tory of the Jewish people affected the course 
of Hebrew literature for children. It was only 
after the education given to Jewish children 
in the Land of Israel had become Westernized 
that the literature written locally for Jewish 
children and adolescents became similar to that 
of Europe and America, a development with 
its advantages and disadvantages. Before the 
advent of Zionism and the revival of Hebrew 
as an everyday language Jewish children only 
read the Torah in Hebrew. Literary materials 
outside holy scripture were only available in 
primitive form, through oral traditions in the 
local language. Hebrew children’s literature 
began with Ze±ev Ya≠veß, whose book תוחיש 
םדק ינמ »i≤ot mini qedem ‘Tales from the Ori-
ent’, written in biblical style, was published in 
Warsaw in 1887. He was gradually joined by 
Yehuda Zvi Levin, Yehuda Steinberg, S. Ben-
Zion, H. N. Bialik, and a few other writers

of their generation who wrote for children. 
Children’s newspapers in Hebrew also ﬁrst 
appeared at this time.
The style of these pioneering authors was 
inﬂuenced by the ancient Hebrew sources; this 
was their strength, and also their weakness. 
Their language was uniform and normative 
for the most part (although Levin Kipnis’ early 
poems, for example, already contain some ele-
ments of spoken Hebrew and show a desire to 
speak to children in their own language). Inter-
estingly enough, although H. N. Bialik belongs 
to the early Modern Hebrew period, when the 
conventions still dictated that texts for children 
be formulated in an elevated register, his own 
works do contain many allusions and (mostly 
covert) ambiguities that point to additional lev-
els in his children’s books, levels not necessarily 
intended for children (Shamir 1986).
Gradually, as the Jewish community in the 
Land of Israel grew, the ﬁgure of the רבצ ßabar 
‘prickly pear; Sabra, a Jew born in the Land of 
Israel’ became predominant in children’s litera-
ture. Until the 1960s in particular ‘mobilized’ 
poetry was quite common; it stressed the values 
of work, defense of the homeland, agriculture, 
the ﬁgure of the Sabra, and the like. The lan-
guage in that period was normative for the 
most part, quite elevated in fact. As we shall see 
below, there are differences in both style and 
content between the children’s poems written 
by Bialik and his followers, Shlonsky, Alter-
man, and Goldberg, and the poets of the 1980s, 
such as Yehonatan Gefen and Nurit Zar™i.
From about the 1960s the psychologistic 
approach came to inﬂuence children’s litera-
ture, which as a result of this and of the inﬂu-
ence of adult literature, began to focus on the 
child as an individual. Authors of children’s 
books put words and expressions typical of 
child language in the mouths of their child 
characters, in contrast to the language of the 
parents, who are presented as speaking in a 
more elevated and normative language. For 
example, in Miriam Yelen-Shtekelis’ poem

According to Shlonsky, Goldberg, and oth-
ers, all genres of children’s literature should 
adhere to a number of rules: texts written for 
children should be appropriate to the age of 
the intended readers and their vocabulary, but 
should not be couched in ‘childish’ language; 
and they should contain educational messages, 
but avoid too much complexity. These prin-
ciples can most clearly be seen in operation 
in poetry for children, where they are perhaps 
more easily applied than in other genres.
Even today children’s literature is written 
in a more normative language than literature 
aimed at adults. Poems for children even retain 
rhyme, and until the 1980s such poems pre-
served stanza and metric structure. These ele-
ments make it easier for the young readers to 
assimilate the poem, and therefore most works 
intended for infants today rhyme, even in prose. 
Indeed, Ephraim Sidon (in an interview he gave 
on 16 October 2009) described his own work 
as follows: “When I write for children I try to

Which I do less, let’s say, in a newspaper. You 
know that tomorrow they’ll use it to wrap 
parsley or salted ﬁsh. Not that I care, but if I 
happen to produce an inelegant rhyme I won’t 
go to court about it. In children’s books I try to 
produce something of the highest quality. That 
is very important to me”.
Modern Hebrew has a very rich children’s lit-
erature. Children’s books are in great demand, 
and are enjoyed and quoted by adults as well, 
perhaps due to the inﬂuence of English-lan-
guage literature (in American literature there is 
no separate category of children’s poetry, but 
prose works are adapted to different ages and 
the speciﬁc problems of the intended audience). 
Modern writers of children’s literature, espe-
cially those whose best works are in this ﬁeld, 
love to play with language, create allusions to 
other texts, and produce ad hoc neologisms, 
particularly in works intended for infants, most 
often in poetry, but also in prose. These texts 
contain a great deal of humor, occasionally 
even irony, intended for the adult who selects 
the book and reads it to the child. Humor is a 
very important element in this sort of literature; 
children are attracted to humor, which can be 
used to convey messages in an indirect manner. 
Shlonsky (1960) was of the opinion that humor 
and the use of child language and children’s 
street songs in works for children, together 
with the rich vocabulary with which children 
can be made acquainted in such works, can give 
rise to an interaction between writer and child. 
This is indeed what he did in his own writings 
for children. ≠Omer Hillel followed in his foot-
steps and so expanded the use of word games 
in his texts to the point that he crossed over 
into nonsense. Indeed, nonsense has penetrated 
into children’s literature, especially in works 
intended for infants; it can be found in particu-
lar in the stories of ≠Oded Burla and the poems 
of Nurit Zar™i. Composers of children’s lit-
erature are very clearly enamored of writing in 
this genre, which allows them to give full vent 
to their creative urges. It is therefore fair to say 
(following Baruch and Fruchtman 1982) that 
written texts for children, especially for infants, 
constitute ‘literary texts’ in the full sense of the 
term, and, like any other work of literature, 
require the tools of textual analysis. Though 
literature intended for children is by its nature 
subject to restrictions due to its educational and 
didactic aims, and so is directed speciﬁcally at 
certain age groups and levels of comprehension, 
as required by an audience of children, a good 
children’s book is ﬁrst of all a work of litera-
ture; it deals with themes that interest children 
and adolescents, but it is written by an adult, 
whose personality and modes of expression ﬁnd 
their way into his or her writings and address 
adult readers as well.
Baruch and Fruchtman (1982) note three 
ways in which children’s poetry enriches its 
readers’ vocabulary. First of all, it adds new 
and unfamiliar words to the child’s lexicon in 
a transparent way that makes their denotation 
very clear; secondly, the new word may be 
introduced as a synonym, occasionally accom-
panied by a clear meta-linguistic statement, 
(e.g., ןועמ םג םיארוק תיבל le-bayit qor±im gam 
ma≠on ‘a bayit [house, home] is also called 
ma≠on [dwelling]’); thirdly, the text provides 
additional meanings to homonymic and polyse-
mic words, e.g., ליג gil, which can mean either 
‘age’ or ‘joy’, as well as new and unfamiliar 
connotations to familiar words, e.g., הנוי yona 
‘dove’ as a symbol of peace. Writers of chil-
dren’s books, just like those who write for 
adults, occasionally invent new words for the 
speciﬁc purposes of their composition (which 
may, however, also eventually enter the lexicon 
of general usage). ≠Omer Hillel and many later

Texts written for adolescents and adults 
show less linguistic creativity than literature 
aimed at infants. What innovation there is 
focuses mainly on distinct themes addressed 
in works on love, domestic crises, problems 
at school, broken taboos, how to treat people 
who are different, and so on. The language of 
such works is mostly quite standard, except 
for colloquial passages in which the adolescent 
himself is the speaker (stories in fact often have 
the protagonist relating his or her story in the 
ﬁrst person). In such stories repetitions abound, 
for emphasis and in order to clarify concepts. 
While literature for adolescents does include 
books of entertainment and mystery stories like 
adult literature, they are either presented within 
the context of the above-mentioned themes or 
are meant to extend the bounds of the imagina-
tion. Humor is often concentrated in works 
of an overall humoristic nature, in which the 
language is terse, and books that are based 
on comics or diaries, in which one is free to 
write in any style one wishes. Nevertheless, the 
‘Dear Diary’ type is usually couched in quite 
normative language and does not descend into 
vulgarities.
As we proceed into the second decade of the 
21st century it is quite clear that the electronic 
media, which has already greatly affected litera-
ture as a whole, will also have a growing impact 
on children’s literature, although experience 
has shown that the literature on which parents, 
and even grandparents, were raised still domi-
nates the market for children’s books in Israel, 
and that writing of linguistically rich quality 
will always retain its inﬂuence. It is therefore 
conceivable that present developments will not 
have a drastic effect on texts written for chil-
dren in the future.

China
There is no evidence that classical Hebrew was 
ever used in China as a living language. It has, 
however, been used as a liturgical language 
among Jewish communities in China. In addi-
tion, Judeo-Persian documents, written in the 
Hebrew script, have been found along the Silk 
Road, evidence of Jewish merchants travelling 
to China.
The earliest written sources that mention 
Jews in China are in Arabic (Leslie 1998:49–
51). Jewish and Russian traders, the Rad-
hânites, visited China in the 9th century C.E. 
Jews were among the many foreigners said to 
have been slaughtered in 878/879 in Khânfû 
(Canton, Guangzhou) (Leslie 1998:15). The 
earliest Chinese historical sources that refer 
to Jews are from the Mongol Yuan dynasty 
(1279–1368). The writings of Marco Polo con-
tain the earliest references by a foreigner to
